questions.stem: Why does the spectrum of a star show dark absorption lines?
options: Dust between the star and Earth blocks every wavelength except a few bright ones
Earth's atmosphere reflects certain wavelengths of starlight back out into space
Cooler gas in the star's outer layers absorbs particular wavelengths
The star's hot core emits light only at particular wavelengths and none in between
questions.explanation: Light from the hot interior has a continuous spectrum. As it passes through cooler gas in the star's atmosphere, atoms absorb photons whose energies match their energy level gaps, leaving dark lines. Each element's lines are at its own wavelengths, so the lines reveal composition.

questions.stem: Which three properties of a star can be found from its spectrum?
options: Surface temperature, composition and velocity towards or away from Earth
Surface temperature, age and the number of planets orbiting it
Chemical composition, mass and distance from the centre of the galaxy
Velocity across the sky, core temperature and the number of its sunspots
questions.explanation: The peak wavelength and the pattern of lines give the surface temperature, the absorption lines identify the elements present, and a Doppler shift of the lines shows motion along the line of sight. Motion across the sky, planets and age are not read directly from a single spectrum.

questions.stem: The absorption lines in a star's spectrum appear at slightly longer wavelengths than the same lines measured in a laboratory. What does this show?
options: The star is moving away from Earth
The star is moving towards Earth
The star is hotter than the Sun
The star contains different elements
questions.explanation: A shift of the whole line pattern to longer wavelengths is a redshift, caused by the source moving away (the Doppler effect). Motion towards us gives a blueshift. A change of composition would change which lines appear, not shift the same lines together.

questions.stem: A star's continuous spectrum peaks at 414 nm. Using Wien's law, what is its surface temperature?
questions.explanation: T = b/λmax = 2.898 × 10⁻³/4.14 × 10⁻⁷ = 7.0 × 10³ K, somewhat hotter than the Sun. Using the wavelength in nanometres gives 7.0 × 10⁻⁶ K, and inverting the formula gives 1.4 × 10⁻⁴ K.

questions.stem: Two stars are seen side by side: one looks red and the other blue-white. What can be concluded?
options: The blue-white star must be much closer to Earth
The blue-white star has the hotter surface
The red star has the higher surface temperature
The red star is moving away from Earth much faster
questions.explanation: A star's colour depends on where its black-body curve peaks, and hotter stars peak at shorter wavelengths, so blue-white stars are hotter than red ones. The small Doppler shifts of nearby stars do not change their colour noticeably, and colour does not indicate distance.

questions.stem: What did Cecilia Payne-Gaposchkin show in her analysis of stellar spectra in the 1920s?
options: Stars are mostly hydrogen and helium, and spectral differences come mainly from temperature
Stars have about the same composition as Earth, with iron the most abundant element
Stars shine by burning coal-like fuels, and their spectra show carbon and oxygen
Stars are moving away from each other, and the universe is expanding
questions.explanation: Applying the new physics of ionisation (the Saha equation) to stellar spectra, Payne-Gaposchkin showed that differences between star types are mostly due to temperature, which sets how strongly each element's lines appear. Correcting for this showed that stars are overwhelmingly hydrogen and helium, overturning the belief that they resembled Earth.

questions.stem: Why was temperature the key to Payne-Gaposchkin's spectral analysis technique?
options: Temperature sets the speed of the star, so it decides how far its spectral lines are Doppler shifted
Temperature decides which elements exist in a star, so hot stars contain no hydrogen at all
Temperature determines the star's distance, so it was needed to correct the brightness of each line
Temperature controls ionisation and excitation, so line strength depends on it as well as abundance
questions.explanation: An element's absorption lines are strong only if many of its atoms are in the right ionisation state and energy level, which depends on temperature. By accounting for this, she could convert line strengths into true abundances. Weak hydrogen lines in some stars reflect temperature, not a lack of hydrogen.

questions.stem: How do the spectra of distant galaxies provide evidence that the universe is expanding?
options: Their spectra become brighter over time as the galaxies move closer to us
Their spectral lines are redshifted, and more distant galaxies have larger redshifts
Their spectral lines are blueshifted, and more distant galaxies have larger blueshifts
Their spectra contain new elements that are not found in nearby galaxies
questions.explanation: Almost all distant galaxies show redshifts, meaning they are receding, and the redshift increases with distance. This pattern, noted by Hubble, is what is expected if space itself is expanding, with galaxies moving apart from each other.

questions.stem: Galaxy A is twice as far away as galaxy B. In an expanding universe, how would their redshifts compare?
options: Galaxy A has about twice the redshift of galaxy B
Galaxy A has about half the redshift of galaxy B
Both galaxies have the same redshift
Galaxy A is blueshifted and galaxy B is redshifted
questions.explanation: Observations show that recession speed, and so redshift, is roughly proportional to distance for galaxies that are not too far away. A galaxy twice as distant recedes about twice as fast. Equal redshifts would mean all galaxies recede at the same speed, which is not observed.

questions.stem: On a Hertzsprung-Russell (H-R) diagram, what is usually plotted on each axis?
options: Luminosity upward, and surface temperature decreasing to the right
Luminosity upward, and surface temperature increasing to the right
Mass upward, and age increasing to the right
Distance upward, and colour from red to blue to the right
questions.explanation: An H-R diagram plots luminosity (or absolute magnitude) against surface temperature (or spectral class), with temperature decreasing from left to right. So hot blue stars are on the left and cool red stars on the right.

questions.stem: Where on an H-R diagram are red supergiants found, and what does this show about them?
options: Bottom right: cool and faint, so they must be very far away
Top right: cool but very luminous, so they must be enormous
Bottom left: hot but faint, so they must be very small
Top left: hot and very luminous, so they must be very young
questions.explanation: Red supergiants are cool, yet among the most luminous stars. A cool surface emits relatively little energy per square metre, so to be so luminous they must have enormous surface areas and radii. Distance does not appear on an H-R diagram, which uses intrinsic luminosity.

questions.stem: White dwarfs lie at the bottom left of an H-R diagram. What does this tell us about them?
options: They are hot but have low luminosity, so they must be very small
They are cool and have very low luminosity, so they must be very old
They are hot and very luminous, so they must be very massive
They are cool but very luminous, so they must be very large
questions.explanation: A star on the left is hot, and one near the bottom has low luminosity. A hot surface radiates strongly per square metre, so a star that is hot yet faint must have a tiny surface area. White dwarfs are about the size of Earth.

questions.stem: What is the correct order of the main spectral classes, from hottest to coolest?
options: A, B, F, G, K, M, O
O, A, B, F, G, M, K
O, B, A, F, G, K, M
M, K, G, F, A, B, O
questions.explanation: The spectral sequence runs O, B, A, F, G, K, M from hottest (blue) to coolest (red). The Sun is a G-type star with a surface temperature of about 5800 K.

questions.stem: Two stars have the same surface temperature, but star P is 100 times more luminous than star Q. What can be concluded?
options: Star P is closer to Earth than star Q
Star P is much younger than star Q
Star P has a larger radius than star Q
Star P has a smaller radius than star Q
questions.explanation: With the same surface temperature, each square metre of both stars emits the same power. Star P can only be more luminous if it has more surface area, so it is larger, perhaps a giant compared with a main-sequence star. Luminosity is intrinsic, so distance does not affect it.

questions.stem: Where is the Sun on an H-R diagram?
options: On the main sequence, at the top left
On the main sequence, near the middle
Among the giants, at the top right
Among the white dwarfs, at the bottom left
questions.explanation: The Sun is a G-type main-sequence star, roughly in the middle of the main sequence in both temperature and luminosity. The top left of the main sequence holds hot, luminous, massive O and B stars.

questions.stem: How does a main-sequence star form?
options: A gas cloud collapses under gravity and heats until hydrogen fusion begins in its core
A gas cloud expands under its own pressure and cools until helium begins to condense
Two planets collide, and the heat of the impact starts nuclear fission in the debris
A white dwarf gathers extra hydrogen from space until its core begins to burn again
questions.explanation: Gravity pulls a cloud of gas and dust together. As it contracts, gravitational potential energy becomes thermal energy and the core temperature rises. When the core is hot and dense enough, hydrogen fusion begins and the outward pressure halts the collapse.

questions.stem: Why does a main-sequence star stay a stable size for most of its life?
options: Fusion produces no pressure, so the star's size depends only on its total mass
The star's rotation flings out exactly as much gas as gravity pulls back in
The outward pressure from fusion energy balances the inward pull of gravity
Gravity has become too weak at that size to compress the star any further
questions.explanation: Energy released by hydrogen fusion in the core keeps the gas hot, and its pressure pushes outward. On the main sequence this balances gravity's inward pull, a state called hydrostatic equilibrium. If fusion slowed, gravity would compress and heat the core until the balance was restored.

questions.stem: How does a main-sequence star's mass determine its position on an H-R diagram?
options: More massive stars are hotter and more luminous, so they lie higher and further left
More massive stars are cooler and fainter, so they lie further down and to the right
More massive stars are hotter but fainter, so they lie further down and to the left
Mass has little effect, as main-sequence position depends mainly on a star's age
questions.explanation: A greater mass compresses the core more strongly, raising its temperature and fusion rate. The star is therefore more luminous and has a hotter surface, placing it higher and further left on the main sequence.

questions.stem: Compared with the Sun, how long does a main-sequence star of ten solar masses remain on the main sequence?
options: Much more time, because it has ten times as much fuel to use
Exactly ten times as long, because lifetime is proportional to mass
The same time, because all main-sequence stars burn for equal lengths of time
Much less time, because it uses its fuel at a far greater rate
questions.explanation: The massive star has more hydrogen, but its luminosity is thousands of times greater, so it uses its fuel far faster and stays on the main sequence for only tens of millions of years. The Sun's main-sequence lifetime is about 10 billion years.

questions.stem: What is the overall result of the proton-proton chain in a main-sequence star?
options: Two helium nuclei are converted into one beryllium nucleus, releasing energy
One carbon nucleus is converted into three helium nuclei, absorbing energy
Four hydrogen nuclei are converted into two deuterium nuclei, absorbing energy
Four hydrogen nuclei are converted into one helium-4 nucleus, releasing energy
questions.explanation: In the proton-proton chain, four protons are fused, step by step, into one helium-4 nucleus, with two positrons and two neutrinos also released. The final helium nucleus has less mass than the four protons, and the mass difference, about 26.7 MeV in total, is released as energy.

questions.stem: The first step of the proton-proton chain is ¹H + ¹H → ²H + e⁺ + ν. Why does this step include a positron?
options: One proton turns into a neutron by the weak force, so charge is carried away by a positron
One neutron turns into a proton by the strong force, so charge is carried away by a positron
The two protons annihilate each other, so their energy reappears as a positron and a neutrino
A deuterium nucleus has charge +2, so a positron must be absorbed to balance the charge
questions.explanation: A deuterium nucleus contains one proton and one neutron, so one of the original protons must become a neutron. That is a weak-force process, which emits a positron to conserve charge and a neutrino. Being slow, this step controls the rate of the whole chain.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the CNO cycle?
options: Hydrogen is fused into carbon, nitrogen and oxygen, and it dominates in stars like the Sun
Carbon is used up to make helium, and it dominates in white dwarfs and neutron stars
Carbon catalyses the fusion of hydrogen into helium, and it dominates in hotter, more massive stars
Carbon, nitrogen and oxygen are fused into iron, and it dominates in the cooler, less massive stars
questions.explanation: In the CNO cycle, carbon-12 captures protons and passes through nitrogen and oxygen isotopes before being restored, while four protons become one helium-4 nucleus. Because the carbon nuclei have a higher charge, the cycle needs higher core temperatures, so it dominates in main-sequence stars more massive than the Sun.

questions.stem: The final step of the CNO cycle is ¹⁵N + ¹H → ¹²C + ⁴He. Why is carbon described as a catalyst in the cycle?
options: The carbon-12 is the product of the cycle, so its amount steadily grows
The carbon-12 that starts the cycle is returned at the end, so it is not used up
The carbon-12 is destroyed at the end, so new carbon must be supplied each time
The carbon-12 releases all the energy itself, so the hydrogen is not needed
questions.explanation: The cycle begins with carbon-12 capturing a proton and ends by releasing carbon-12 again, along with a helium-4 nucleus. The net effect is the same as the proton-proton chain: four protons into one helium nucleus. The carbon makes the process possible without being consumed.

questions.stem: Which main-sequence stars produce most of their energy by the proton-proton chain?
options: Only white dwarfs and neutron stars
Only red supergiants at the end of their lives
The Sun and stars of lower mass
Only stars far more massive than the Sun
questions.explanation: The proton-proton chain works at lower core temperatures, so it dominates in the Sun and smaller main-sequence stars. Hotter cores in more massive main-sequence stars favour the CNO cycle. White dwarfs and neutron stars no longer fuse hydrogen.

questions.stem: When a star of about one solar mass runs out of hydrogen in its core, what happens next?
options: Its core expands and cools, and it moves down and to the left on the H-R diagram
Its core contracts and heats, its outer layers expand and cool, and it becomes a red giant
Its core explodes immediately as a supernova, leaving behind a black hole where it was
It cools and fades straight away into a white dwarf, without any further fusion taking place
questions.explanation: Without core fusion, gravity compresses the helium core, which heats up. Hydrogen fuses in a shell around it, and the outer layers swell and cool, so the star moves up and to the right on the H-R diagram as a red giant. A one-solar-mass star does not become a supernova.

questions.stem: What is the final stage of a star of about one solar mass?
options: A white dwarf, after shedding its outer layers as a planetary nebula
A black hole, after its core collapses at the end of its red giant stage
A neutron star, after it explodes as a supernova
A red supergiant that keeps fusing heavier elements for ever
questions.explanation: After its red giant stages, a Sun-like star puffs off its outer layers as a planetary nebula, leaving its hot carbon-oxygen core as a white dwarf. The white dwarf no longer fuses and slowly cools. Neutron stars and black holes come from much more massive stars.

questions.stem: Which sequence describes the evolution, after the main sequence, of a star of about 15 solar masses?
options: Red supergiant, fusion of successively heavier elements to iron, core collapse supernova, neutron star or black hole
Red giant, planetary nebula, white dwarf, then a slow cooling to a dark, cold object over billions of years
White dwarf, red giant, supernova, then a return to the main sequence as a new star
Red supergiant, fusion of iron into uranium, planetary nebula, then a white dwarf made mainly of uranium
questions.explanation: A massive star becomes a red supergiant and fuses heavier and heavier elements in shells, ending with an iron core. Iron fusion cannot release energy, so the core collapses and the star explodes as a supernova, leaving a neutron star or, for the most massive cores, a black hole.

questions.stem: Where on the H-R diagram does a Sun-like star move when it leaves the main sequence and becomes a red giant?
options: Down and to the right: fainter and cooler
Straight up: more luminous at the same temperature
Up and to the right: more luminous and cooler
Down and to the left: fainter and hotter
questions.explanation: As a red giant the star's outer layers expand enormously, so its surface cools (moving right) while its total luminosity rises because of its huge surface area (moving up). Later, as a white dwarf, it ends at the bottom left.

questions.stem: In the core of a red giant, helium is fused into carbon. Why must the core be much hotter than a main-sequence core for this to happen?
options: Helium fusion absorbs energy, so extra heat must be supplied from outside
Carbon can only exist at high temperatures, so it would fall apart in a cool core
Helium nuclei have twice the charge of protons, so they repel more strongly
Helium nuclei are lighter than protons, so they move too slowly when cool
questions.explanation: Each helium nucleus has a charge of +2, so the electrostatic repulsion between them is greater than between protons. The nuclei need higher speeds, and so a higher temperature (around 100 million K), to get close enough for the strong force to fuse them.

questions.stem: How do changing gravity and fusion pressure allow a massive star to make successively heavier elements?
options: Fusion pressure keeps rising throughout the star's life, which squeezes nuclei together harder
Gravity weakens as the star ages, so heavier nuclei can form without being pulled apart
When each fuel runs out, gravity compresses and heats the core until a heavier fuel can fuse
When each fuel runs out, the core expands and cools, which lets heavier nuclei form more easily
questions.explanation: When a fuel in the core is exhausted, fusion pressure drops and gravity contracts the core, raising its temperature. Eventually it is hot enough to fuse the ash of the previous stage, for example helium into carbon, then carbon into neon and so on, building shells of different elements.

questions.stem: In terms of binding energy, why is iron the heaviest element produced by fusion in the core of a red supergiant?
options: Iron has about the highest binding energy per nucleon, so fusing it absorbs energy
Iron has the lowest binding energy per nucleon, so it falls apart before it can fuse any further
Iron nuclei carry no charge, so the strong force cannot act between two iron nuclei
Iron is the heaviest element that exists, so no heavier nuclei could ever form
questions.explanation: Binding energy per nucleon rises up to a peak near iron and then falls. Fusing lighter nuclei moves towards the peak and releases energy, but fusing iron would move away from it and absorb energy. With no energy to support it, the iron core collapses.

questions.stem: If iron is the limit for fusion in stars, how are elements heavier than iron, such as gold and uranium, made?
options: By fusion of iron nuclei in the cores of red supergiants before they collapse
By fission of even heavier nuclei that were present when the universe began
By hydrogen fusion in the cores of main-sequence stars like the Sun
By neutron capture, particularly in supernovae and other neutron-rich events
questions.explanation: Heavier elements are built by neutron capture: nuclei absorb neutrons, which feel no electrostatic repulsion, and then beta decay into heavier elements. Slow neutron capture happens in giant stars, and rapid capture in supernovae and neutron star mergers. Fusion beyond iron would absorb energy.

questions.stem: Which element do main-sequence stars produce by nuclear fusion in their cores?
options: Carbon
Iron
Hydrogen
Helium
questions.explanation: Main-sequence stars fuse hydrogen into helium, by the proton-proton chain or the CNO cycle. Carbon and heavier elements up to iron are made in later stages, once the core has run out of hydrogen. Hydrogen is the fuel, not the product.

questions.stem: Which object is left after a core-collapse supernova of a very massive star?
options: A main-sequence star of lower mass
A planetary nebula with no core
A neutron star or a black hole
A white dwarf or a red giant
questions.explanation: The collapsing core of a massive star is crushed into a neutron star or, if massive enough, a black hole, while the outer layers are blasted into space. White dwarfs and planetary nebulae come from lower-mass stars like the Sun.

questions.stem: Which force causes a cloud of gas and dust to collapse and form a star?
options: Gravity
The strong force
Magnetism
The weak force
questions.explanation: Gravity pulls the gas and dust inward, and the contraction turns gravitational potential energy into heat. The strong force acts only once nuclei are close enough to fuse, after the core is hot enough.

questions.stem: Star X is on the main sequence at the top left of an H-R diagram, and star Y is on the main sequence at the bottom right. Which comparison is correct?
options: X is more massive, cooler and has a longer main-sequence lifetime than Y
X is less massive, cooler and has a shorter main-sequence lifetime than Y
X is more massive, hotter and has a shorter main-sequence lifetime than Y
X is less massive, hotter and has a longer main-sequence lifetime than Y
questions.explanation: Along the main sequence, position is set by mass: the top left holds massive, hot, luminous stars, which burn their hydrogen quickly and have short lifetimes. Star Y is a cool, faint, low-mass red dwarf, which uses its fuel slowly and stays on the main sequence far longer.
